title: Environment and Gender Justice

cards.h: Problems that do not stop at borders
cards.b:
Climate change, biodiversity loss and gender inequality are problems no single state can solve. They also split the world, between rich and poor states, between past and future polluters, and between men and women inside every society.

The environment is a regular Paper II topic: Stockholm, Rio, Kyoto, Paris, "common but differentiated responsibilities" (CBDR), climate finance and India's stand. Gender justice appears less often, but it links to feminist IR, CEDAW, Beijing and women in peace and security.

This lesson covers both. Treat environment as one half and gender as the other half of the answer, and connect them where you can: women are hit harder by climate impacts, and women's knowledge and leadership matter in natural-resource politics.

The current-affairs layer changes every year. Learn the logic of the negotiations, then add the latest COP in one or two lines.

• Stockholm, June 1972. The first UN conference on the human environment. It led to UNEP. Indira Gandhi's speech said poverty is the greatest polluter.
  • Brundtland Commission, 1987. Our Common Future defined sustainable development as meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
  • Rio Earth Summit, 1992. The UNFCCC, the Convention on Biological Diversity, Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration. Principle 7 states CBDR.
  • Kyoto Protocol. Adopted 1997, in force 2005. Only developed (Annex I) countries had binding cuts.
  • Copenhagen, 2009. Failure to agree a binding deal. A goal of $100 billion a year in climate finance was set.
  • Paris Agreement. Adopted 12 December 2015, in force November 2016.

cards.h: The Paris Agreement and its logic
cards.b:
The Paris Agreement shifted from a top-down to a bottom-up design. Every country puts forward its own pledge, called a Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC).

Main features

  • Goal: keep warming well below 2 degrees C above pre-industrial levels, and pursue efforts for 1.5 degrees C.
  • NDCs are updated every five years, each more ambitious (the "ratchet").
  • A global stocktake every five years. The first concluded at COP28 (2023).
  • Article 6 on carbon markets. Article 8 on loss and damage. Finance, technology and capacity building for developing countries.
  • Applies to all, but keeps CBDR "in the light of different national circumstances".

The weakness: pledges are not legally enforceable, and current pledges fall short. 2024 was the warmest year on record, at about 1.5 degrees C above pre-industrial levels by WMO's estimate.

• COP26, Glasgow (2021). First mention of phasing down unabated coal. India announced its Panchamrit targets and net zero by 2070.
  • COP27, Sharm el-Sheikh (2022). Agreement to set up a loss and damage fund.
  • COP28, Dubai (2023). First global stocktake. The "UAE Consensus" called for transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems.
  • COP29, Baku (2024). The New Collective Quantified Goal: developed countries to lead mobilising at least $300 billion a year by 2035, within a wider call to reach $1.3 trillion from all sources. Developing countries called it too low.
  • COP30, Belem (November 2025). The "Global Mutirao" package called for tripling adaptation finance by 2035. The final text did not carry a formal fossil-fuel roadmap, which a large coalition had sought. Brazil's presidency took that work forward outside the formal decision.
  • COP31, Antalya (9-20 November 2026). Hosted by Turkiye, with Australia leading the negotiations. It is under way at the time of writing.

The US withdrew from the Paris Agreement; the exit took effect in January 2026.

The Global South's case

Rich countries caused most historical emissions. So under CBDR and respective capabilities (CBDR-RC) they must cut first, and provide finance and technology. The right to develop is real. Per capita emissions of many developing states are low.

The developed world's case

Emissions growth now comes from large emerging economies, such as China and India. China is the largest emitter today, though its per capita and historic figures are lower than the US. So all major emitters should share the burden.

Flash points

  • Finance. The $100 billion promise was met late. Adaptation and loss-and-damage funding remain small.
  • Carbon border taxes. The EU's CBAM began its definitive phase on 1 January 2026. India and others call it unfair trade protection.
  • Equity. Concept of a carbon budget shared fairly between countries.

Norms like "polluter pays" and the "precautionary principle" (Rio Principle 15) support the South's case. The "tragedy of the commons" (Garrett Hardin, 1968) explains why collective action is hard.

Gender justice means fair treatment, voice and resources for all genders. It covers rights, safety, work, health, education and political power.

Feminist IR asks "where are the women?" Cynthia Enloe, Bananas, Beaches and Bases (1989), showed how international politics depends on women's often unseen labour, from diplomats' wives to factory and sex workers. J. Ann Tickner, Gender in International Relations (1992), argued that realism's idea of power is shaped by male experience. Later work (Jean Elshtain, Women and War, 1987; Laura Sjoberg) looked at war, security and the state.

Key global instruments

  • 1975 Mexico City: first UN World Conference on Women.
  • CEDAW (1979, in force 1981): the international bill of rights for women.
  • Beijing 1995: the Fourth World Conference. The Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action made gender mainstreaming central.
  • UNSC Resolution 1325 (2000): Women, Peace and Security.
  • SDG 5 (2015): gender equality.
  • UN Women (created 2010).

The link between gender and environment has a long history.

  • Ecofeminism. Vandana Shiva, Staying Alive: Women, Ecology and Development (1988), and Maria Mies and Shiva, Ecofeminism (1993). They argued that the domination of nature and of women are linked, and that modern "development" ignores women's knowledge and subsistence work.
  • Chipko movement (1970s, Uttarakhand). Women villagers, famous through Gaura Devi at Reni (1974), hugged trees to stop felling. It is a core example of a women-led environmental movement.
  • Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt Movement in Kenya (founded 1977). She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004.

Climate impacts are gendered. Women, especially in poor rural areas, depend more on water, fuel and farming. They bear more of the burden after floods and droughts. UN climate talks have therefore adopted a Gender Action Plan.

Critics of ecofeminism say it can treat women as "closer to nature", which is a stereotype. Others call it too general across classes and cultures.

• Weak enforcement. Both climate and gender norms rely on voluntary pledges and reporting. There is no world court for climate compliance.
  • Finance gap. Money for adaptation, loss and damage is far below needs.
  • US retreat. Withdrawal from Paris and cuts in development aid weaken collective action. Funding for gender programmes was also hit by aid cuts in 2025.
  • Fossil fuel lock-in. COP28 and COP30 could only agree on language, not a binding phase-out.
  • Backlash. Women's rights face pushback in some states, for example in Afghanistan under the Taliban.
  • Intersectionality. Black and post-colonial feminists (Kimberle Crenshaw, 1989; Chandra Talpade Mohanty) say "women" is not one group. Class, caste, race and place shape experience.
  • Green colonialism? Some say climate rules (CBAM, conservation zones) bring new burdens on the South.

Positive signs: the cost of solar and wind has fallen sharply, and gender parity in girls' primary schooling has largely been reached.

cards.h: India on climate and on women
cards.b:
Climate.

  • India's stand: climate justice, CBDR-RC and the right to development. Its per capita emissions are far below the global average.
  • Glasgow 2021: Panchamrit and net zero by 2070. Updated NDC (approved by Cabinet on 25 March 2026): about 47% cut in emissions intensity of GDP from the 2005 level by 2035, about 60% of installed power capacity from non-fossil sources, and an added carbon sink of 3.5-4 billion tonnes. Confirm the final numbers in the filed document.
  • International Solar Alliance (2015), Mission LiFE (announced at COP26, 2021), and the National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023).
  • Constitution: Article 48A and 51A(g) (42nd Amendment, 1976); Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.

Gender.

  • Constitution: Articles 14, 15(3) and 39(d); 73rd and 74th Amendments reserve one-third of local seats for women.
  • Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (106th Amendment, 2023) reserves one-third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats, to take effect after the next census and delimitation.
  • India ranked 131 of 145 in the WEF Global Gender Gap Index 2026, doing best in political empowerment.
  • Peacekeeping: India sent the first all-women UN formed police unit to Liberia (2007).

"Discuss the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities in climate negotiations. How has India upheld it?"
"Evaluate the Paris Agreement as compared to the Kyoto Protocol."
"Does climate action impinge on the right to development of the Global South?"
"Explain the contribution of feminist perspectives to the study of international relations."

Structure for climate: milestones (Stockholm, Rio, Kyoto, Paris), CBDR, North-South debate, recent COPs in a line each, India's stand and NDC. End with a way forward: finance, technology transfer, adaptation.

Structure for gender: feminist IR (Enloe, Tickner), CEDAW and Beijing, UNSCR 1325, links to environment (Chipko, ecofeminism), Indian laws and the 106th Amendment.

Keep a balanced conclusion: global goals need both justice and ambition.
